extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claim language for indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (and pre‑AIA §112 second paragraph), including how to construe claims during prosecution, what evidence/record must be created, and appropriate examiner/applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness standard under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of indefiniteness requires whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand the metes and bounds of the claimed invention in view of the specification (citing Power-One; Orthokinetics example). The test is whether the claim informs those skilled in the art of its scope with reasonable certainty (Nautilus for issued patents; see relation to prosecution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, claims are construed by giving them their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification to facilitate sharpening and clarifying claims at the application stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the narrower judicial claim construction used in litigation; apply BRI (citing Packard, Buszard, Yamamoto, Zletz). Recognize this can result in a lower threshold for ambiguity than a court's determination. Use BRI to determine whether metes and bounds are clear; if not, reject under §112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision (particularity and distinctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets the statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision—i.e., particularity and distinctness required by §112(b), not whether better wording exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow claims that define patentable subject matter with the required degree of particularity and distinctness. Permit some latitude in expression when the statutory requirement is nevertheless satisfied. The essential inquiry is whether the claims circumscribe particular subject matter with reasonable clarity and particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual analysis: disclosure, prior art, and POSITA understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of (A) the content of the application disclosure, (B) teachings of the prior art, and (C) the claim interpretation a person of ordinary skill in the art would give at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing claims, consider all three factors together rather than in isolation. The relevant time is before the effective filing date for AIA applications (or at the time of invention for pre‑AIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must view the claim in its entirety and consider the interaction of all limitations to ascertain the inventor’s contribution and whether the claim apprises POSITA of its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not analyze isolated words outside the context of the whole claim; the totality of limitations can resolve apparent ambiguities (citing Larsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness arises if more than one reasonable interpretation exists under BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: If, under the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, a person of ordinary skill would read the claim with more than one reasonable meaning, the claim is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is more than one reasonable interpretation of a claim term or phrase such that the metes and bounds are unclear, a §112(b) rejection is appropriate (citing Packard, Zletz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate claim breadth with indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not necessarily indefinite merely because it covers a wide scope; indefiniteness relates to unclear boundaries, not breadth per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genus claim that clearly delineates scope can be broad but definite; by contrast, a genus claim that leaves ambiguity as to which species are included is indefinite (see Markush guidance at MPEP §2173.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must establish a clear prosecution record when asserting indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a prima facie case of indefiniteness, the examiner should create a complete and accurate application file that explains the basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear explanations of actions in the Office action (citing MPEP §1302.14, §707.07(f)). Avoid mere conclusory statements that a term is indefinite; set forth findings and reasons supporting the rejection to enhance prosecution history clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action content requirement: identify term, explain why, and suggest resolution when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: An Office action rejecting a claim as indefinite must (1) point out the specific term or phrase deemed indefinite, (2) explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and (3) whenever practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness may be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient detail to permit the applicant to prepare a meaningful response. Cite relevant MPEP sections (§706.03, §707.07(g),(d)). Failure of applicant to adequately respond may result in a final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid per se rules; use fact‑specific rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical §112(b) rejections; examples of language held indefinite are fact specific and should not be mechanically applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the illustrative examples in MPEP §2173.05(d) as fact‑specific guidance only, not blanket rules that automatically trigger rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage constructive examiner suggestions but not insistence on preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to improve clarity/precision but should not insist on their own wording if the applicant’s language satisfies §112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer suggested amendments or wording to help applicant resolve issues, but accept other modes of expression that meet statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant options to overcome indefiniteness: amend or provide persuasive evidentiary explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to an indefiniteness rejection applicants may amend the claim or provide persuasive explanation (and evidence as necessary) demonstrating that a POSITA would not find the language unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive explanations may include separate definitions, e.g., art‑recognized dictionary definitions, or other intrinsic/extrinsic evidence to show how a skilled artisan would understand the term (citing Packard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews to attempt resolution when indefiniteness is the only issue
rubrics_metrics.description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, examiners are encouraged to initiate an interview with applicant to discuss claim language, BRI, and possible claim amendments before resorting to a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews can clarify meanings and eliminate the need for a §112(b) rejection. The substance of any interview must be made of record and include why a term is/ is not clear, inconsistency with the specification, whether §112(f) is invoked and corresponding structure, and any discussed amendments (citing MPEP §713.04 and 37 CFR 1.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide claim interpretation in Reasons for Allowance when the prosecution record does not make reasons clear
rubrics_metrics.description: If the file record as a whole does not make clear the reasons for allowing claims, the examiner may set forth the claim interpretation applied in a Reasons for Allowance statement pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting forth claim interpretation improves quality and reliability of issued patents and aids public understanding. However, avoid placing unwarranted interpretations (either broad or narrow) on the claims (citing MPEP §1302.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: When withdrawing or changing position, explain the basis in the next Office communication
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner is persuaded by applicant arguments or amendments and withdraws a prior §112(b) rejection, the examiner should indicate in the next Office communication that the rejection has been withdrawn and explain what prompted the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific reference to applicant remarks or amendments that changed the examiner’s position to enhance prosecution history clarity and assist future interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record estoppel consequences of narrowing §112 amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that a narrowing amendment made to satisfy any Patent Act requirement may give rise to prosecution history estoppel and the examiner should make the record clear regarding §112 amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Festo: determine whether an amendment was cosmetic or narrowing; if narrowing, it may create estoppel. Make explicit reasoning of amendments part of the record to assist later estoppel analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When additional information is necessary, consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines more information is necessary to ascertain the meaning of a claim term, a formal requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP §704.10 for requirements for information and use this procedure when intrinsic evidence is insufficient to resolve claim meaning.
